sentences.text: Governments should tax sugar-sweetened drinks because their health costs are borne not only by consumers but also by publicly funded health systems.
The World Health Organization recommends taxes that raise the retail price of sugary drinks by at least 20% to reduce consumption.
Mexico introduced a one-peso-per-litre tax in 2014; a study published in the BMJ found purchases of taxed drinks fell by an average of 7.6% in its first year, compared with estimated pre-tax trends.
A tax is not a complete solution to diet-related disease, but it is a practical way to discourage excess consumption and help fund prevention.
Your Mexico figure conflates two results: the 2016 BMJ study estimated a 6% purchase reduction in 2014; a subsequent Health Affairs study reported a 7.6% average reduction across 2014–2015.
Neither result establishes a corresponding reduction in obesity or diabetes.
Purchases are an intermediate outcome, not proof that public healthcare savings exceed the policy’s costs.
Moreover, a per-litre tax charges the same amount regardless of the buyer’s income, imposing a larger proportional burden on poorer consumers who continue buying.
Governments should address diet-related disease, but targeting one product with a financially unequal tax requires stronger justification than reduced purchases alone.
You’re right that reduced purchases alone do not prove lower obesity or diabetes, or net healthcare savings.
But a tax need not clear that bar to be justified: it can reduce consumption and raise revenue for prevention.
Mexico’s 7.6% figure comes from a study of average purchases over 2014–2015, not a measured health outcome.

Crucially, that study found larger purchase declines among lower-socioeconomic-status households, which may make health benefits progressive even if the tax itself takes a larger share of poorer consumers’ income.
Governments can use the revenue to offset that burden, for example by funding safe drinking water and health programs in underserved communities.
Larger purchase declines among poorer households do not establish progressive health benefits; your wording correctly makes those benefits conditional.
Nor does raising revenue demonstrate that this particular tax is preferable to funding prevention through broader, more progressive taxation.
Avoidance also complicates the evidence: a 2019 JAMA study of Philadelphia’s beverage tax found that increased sales in bordering areas partially offset reduced sales within the city.
Revenue-funded water and health programs may be worthwhile, but their value does not automatically justify their funding mechanism.
Governments should assess actual health gains, distributional costs, and alternatives—not treat reduced local purchases and promised spending as sufficient justification.

Border shopping is a real limitation, but it does not erase the evidence: the 2019 JAMA study found Philadelphia’s tax reduced sales within the city, while increased sales in nearby areas partially offset that decline.
That points to a case for wider coordination, not abandoning the policy.
Nor must a drink tax replace progressive taxation; governments can use both, directing revenue to water access and prevention where burdens fall hardest.
The standard should be whether a tax is a useful, adjustable tool—not whether it alone proves lower disease rates or beats every alternative.
WHO recommends taxing sugary drinks to raise prices by at least 20% as one measure to reduce consumption.
Wider coordination may reduce border shopping, but it does not resolve the unequal financial burden or demonstrate health gains.

Philadelphia’s tax, introduced in 2017 at 1.5 cents per ounce, covers artificially sweetened beverages as well as sugary ones: its reach illustrates why “beverage tax” and “targeted health intervention” are not interchangeable.
WHO’s recommendation supports your position, but cannot establish that every proposed tax is well designed.
We need not demand that a tax cure disease alone; we should demand evidence that its expected benefits justify its burdens.
Funding water access and prevention remains worthwhile without making this particular revenue source necessary.
Sugar-sweetened drinks add calories without providing the fullness of solid food, and high consumption contributes to obesity and type 2 diabetes.
Governments should tax them to reduce consumption and help cover the resulting public-health costs.

This is more than theory: after Mexico introduced a nationwide 10% tax on sugary drinks in 2014, purchases of taxed beverages fell by an average of 7.6% over the first two years compared with the expected trend, according to a 2017 study in *BMJ*.
A well-designed tax can also fund health programs, while leaving consumers free to choose what they drink.
Mexico's 7.6% drop is modest and largely offset by substitutions to untaxed high-calorie drinks, so total calories barely change.
Taxes are regressive: the poorest households spend a larger share of income on beverages and pay more, while wealthier consumers barely notice.
Denmark repealed its fat tax in 2012 after 15 months, citing administrative costs and cross-border shopping.
Philadelphia's 2017 beverage tax cut city sales, but nearby purchases rose, showing leakage.
The UK's Soft Drinks Industry Levy cut sugar in drinks, yet Year 6 child obesity rose from 20.1% in 2017/18 to 22.7% in 2022/23.
A tax that shifts purchases without improving health is bad policy.

The Mexico study did not find that substitution erased the decline: purchases of untaxed beverages rose only slightly, while purchases of taxed drinks fell by 7.6% on average and more among lower-income households.
Denmark’s repealed policy was a tax on saturated fat, not sugary drinks, so it is not a direct test of this motion.

Nor does rising child obesity in England show the Soft Drinks Industry Levy failed: Public Health England reported that the average sugar content of soft drinks subject to the levy fell by 29% between 2015 and 2018.
A tax is not a complete obesity policy, but directing its revenue to health programs can help offset its burden on poorer households.
You are right that Denmark was a fat tax, so I drop it.
But Mexico's BMJ study tracked purchases, not obesity or diabetes; no outcome improved.
Philadelphia's 1.5-cent-per-ounce tax (2017) cut city sales 38%, while a 2020 JAMA Internal Medicine study found nearby sales rose 15.6%, so leakage erased much of the effect.
England's levy cut sugar 29% by 2018, yet Year 6 obesity rose from 20.1% in 2017/18 to 22.7% in 2022/23.
A regressive tax that shifts purchases and fails to improve health is not justified.
Revenue does not fix that.

The Philadelphia evidence does not show leakage erased the effect: a 2020 study in *JAMA Internal Medicine* estimated that combined purchases in Philadelphia and nearby areas still fell after the tax.
And a tax need not reverse an epidemic on its own to be justified.
England’s rising obesity figures reflect many influences; meanwhile, the levy prompted manufacturers to reformulate drinks, reducing sugar exposure even for people who did not change brands.
Taxes are imperfect, but evidence of lower sugary-drink purchases and lower sugar content supports them as one tool alongside broader prevention.
Revenue can also fund programs that benefit communities bearing the greatest health burden.
You say combined Philadelphia purchases fell, but even if true, the tax still takes a larger share of income from poor families.
More importantly, no study links these taxes to reduced obesity or diabetes.
Mexico's 7.6% purchase decline tracked purchases only, not health.
England's levy cut sugar 29% by 2018, yet Year 6 obesity rose from 20.1% in 2017/18 to 22.7% in 2022/23.
A regressive tax that fails to improve health outcomes is not justified.
Revenue does not cure that; it just moves money from poor families to government programs.
Countries should build more nuclear plants because they can produce large amounts of electricity with very low lifecycle emissions, including during periods when wind and solar output is low.
The IPCC’s Fifth Assessment Report gives median lifecycle emissions of about 12 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for nuclear power, compared with about 820 grams for coal.
France illustrates the potential: nuclear supplied roughly two-thirds of its electricity in 2023, according to the International Energy Agency.
New plants are costly and take time to build, so they are not the only climate solution.
But alongside renewables, nuclear can replace fossil-fuel generation with reliable low-carbon power.
Building nuclear plants is a slow and costly way to cut emissions.
The Vogtle expansion in Georgia cost over $30 billion and came online years behind schedule.
Lazard’s 2024 analysis shows new nuclear at $142–222 per megawatt-hour, while utility-scale solar and onshore wind cost $29–92 and $27–73 respectively.
That money buys far more clean power if spent on renewables, storage and grid upgrades, and delivers reductions sooner.
Nuclear also leaves unresolved high-level waste and carries accident and proliferation risks.
For rapid, affordable decarbonization, countries should not prioritize new nuclear.
Vogtle shows that nuclear projects can be delayed and expensive; it does not show that every country should reject them.
Lazard’s figures compare plant-level costs, not the full cost of keeping electricity reliable when wind and solar output is low, including storage, transmission and backup.
Nuclear plants can supply low-carbon power around the clock for decades, complementing renewables rather than competing with them.
Waste and accident risks deserve strict regulation, but they are manageable policy challenges, not reasons to rely on fossil fuels.
Countries should choose projects carefully and build nuclear where it can deliver dependable emissions cuts.
Your Vogtle point is not isolated: Flamanville 3 in France began construction in 2007 and only connected to the grid in 2024, with costs roughly four times the initial estimate.
That delay means nuclear cannot deliver the near-term emissions cuts the next decade requires.
On system costs, nuclear carries hidden burdens that plant-level LCOE figures understate, not overstate: long construction financing, decommissioning, liability caps, and fuel-cycle risks.
Renewables plus storage, demand response, and transmission can be built faster and cheaper in most markets.
Calling waste and accident risks “manageable” ignores that no permanent repository for high-level commercial waste has opened after seventy years.
We should not lock in slow, costly nuclear.
Flamanville is a real warning about cost and schedule, but it does not prove nuclear is unsuitable everywhere.
Renewables can often be built faster; they still need a reliable system when their output is low.
The IEA identifies nuclear as the world’s second-largest source of low-emissions electricity, after hydropower.

Waste is a serious responsibility, but it is not accurate to say no country is addressing it: Finland is building the Onkalo deep geological repository, with operations expected to begin in the coming years.
Countries should accelerate renewables and grids while building nuclear where it can provide dependable low-carbon power.
Your Onkalo point is overstated: Finland’s repository is not yet operating, and no country has begun final disposal of commercial high-level waste.
Being second-largest existing low-emissions source does not justify new plants, which face cost overruns and decade-long delays.
Flamanville and Vogtle are representative, not exceptions: nuclear construction consistently misses schedules and budgets.
The reliability gap can be met faster and cheaper with renewables, storage, demand response, and stronger grids, which are deployable now, not in the 2030s or 2040s.
Countries should spend scarce decarbonization funds where they cut emissions soonest and at lowest system cost.
Countries should build more nuclear power plants because cutting emissions requires replacing fossil fuels with reliable, low-carbon electricity.
The IPCC’s 2014 assessment reported median life-cycle emissions of 12 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for nuclear power, compared with 820 for coal and 490 for natural gas.
Those figures include construction and fuel supply, not just plant operation.
Nuclear plants can generate electricity regardless of whether the sun shines or wind blows.
New reactors should complement renewables, not compete with them.
Where countries can finance and regulate them effectively, excluding nuclear unnecessarily narrows the options for decarbonization.
PRO's low-carbon figure is real, but new nuclear is too slow and costly to cut emissions now.
Vogtle Units 3 and 4 began in 2009, cost over $30 billion against a $14 billion budget, and finished in 2023 and 2024.
Olkiluoto 3 in Finland started in 2005 and only entered service in 2023.
Flamanville 3 cost €19 billion.
Lazard's 2024 analysis puts nuclear at $142–$222 per megawatt-hour, versus $29–$92 for utility solar.
That capital would cut more carbon faster through renewables, storage, and efficiency.
Permanent waste storage remains unresolved, as Yucca Mountain's 2010 defunding shows.
Those overruns are serious, but they do not establish that every nuclear program must repeat them.
The United Arab Emirates began construction at Barakah in 2012; all four reactors were commercially operating by September 2024, with 5.6 gigawatts of capacity.
Lazard’s generation-cost comparison does not establish the cost of supplying electricity around the clock: solar alone cannot provide that service.
Renewables and efficiency should expand immediately, while nuclear addresses longer-term needs.
Yucca Mountain’s failure is not proof that disposal is technically impossible: Sweden’s government approved a deep geological repository at Forsmark in January 2022.
Nuclear deserves selective investment, not blanket exclusion.
Barakah is real but singular: a petro-state, one utility, imported Korean reactors, and expatriate labor.
It doesn’t rescue projects facing democratic siting fights.
Lazard’s own 2024 solar-plus-storage range starts at $60 per megawatt-hour, below nuclear’s $142 floor.
Sweden approved Forsmark in 2022, but no spent fuel is disposed there yet, and Finland’s Onkalo isn’t routinely operating.
Most countries still lack repositories.
New reactors take a decade or more and crowd out cheaper, faster cuts.
Renewables, storage, transmission, and efficiency should lead; nuclear is a costly detour, not the answer.
Solar-plus-storage’s starting price does not establish the cost of reliable supply through prolonged low-wind, low-sun periods; storage duration matters.
Nor does Barakah need to represent every country: this motion supports building where conditions are suitable, not everywhere indiscriminately.
Nuclear construction need not always exceed a decade: South Korea’s Shin Kori 3 began construction in 2008 and entered commercial operation in 2016.
Sweden’s repository approval does not mean disposal has begun, but it demonstrates progress beyond Yucca Mountain’s political impasse.
Renewables, transmission, and efficiency should lead immediate cuts.
That is compatible with building nuclear for durable, low-carbon supply rather than continuing fossil dependence.
PRO cites Shin Kori 3's eight-year build, but that required Korea's state-owned utility, standardized design, and a single site.
Most democracies face siting and legal delays.
Even eight years misses 2030 targets.
Lazard's solar-plus-storage at $60 per megawatt-hour undercuts nuclear's $142 floor; overbuilding solar and wind plus transmission handles low-wind periods at lower cost.
Sweden's repository is approved but not operating; waste remains unresolved globally.
Given the climate emergency, capital should go to proven rapid cuts, not costly detours.
Nuclear is not necessary.
Sugar-sweetened drinks are a proven driver of obesity and diabetes, and taxes curb consumption.
Mexico’s one-peso-per-litre tax, in force since January 2014, cut purchases of taxed beverages by 5.5% in its first year and 9.7% in the second, according to a 2016 BMJ study.
Berkeley, California’s first US soda tax, adopted in 2014, reduced sugary drink consumption by 21% in low-income neighbourhoods.
The World Health Organization has explicitly endorsed such taxes, recommending they raise retail prices by at least 20%.
Governments already tax tobacco and alcohol to reduce harm; taxing liquid sugar aligns with that evidence-based public health principle.
Reduced purchases are not reduced obesity.
Mexico's tax has run since 2014, yet Mexico remains among the most obese nations in the OECD, and no study has shown the tax reversing national obesity trends.
Consumers substitute other calories, and they shop across borders: Philadelphia's 1.5-cent-per-ounce tax, introduced in 2017, pushed many shoppers to suburban stores outside the city.
These taxes are also regressive, taking a larger share of income from poor households.
Democracies have noticed.
Cook County, Illinois, repealed its penny-per-ounce tax in 2017 after roughly two months, and Denmark abandoned its fat tax and its soft-drink tax after businesses lost sales to Germany and Sweden.
Education, reformulation and healthcare access work without punishing the poor.
You say reduced purchases don't cut obesity.
National obesity is decades in the making; no single tax can reverse it in a few years.
But the BMJ study of Mexico's tax found purchases of taxed beverages fell 9.7% by year two — that's a measurable drop in liquid sugar, the very driver of diabetes.
You call the tax regressive, yet Berkeley's 2014 tax cut consumption by 21% in low-income neighborhoods, precisely the people with the highest obesity burden, so the health benefit is progressive.
Cross-border shopping is a distribution problem, not an argument against state or national levies.
Cook County's repeal followed a well-funded industry campaign, not a scientific defeat.
PRO concedes the core point: the tax has not reversed obesity in Mexico after a decade.
If the payoff is always "decades away," it can never be tested, which is a weak basis for taxing every shopper.
Berkeley's 21% figure came from self-reported street surveys.
The larger 2017 PLOS Medicine study of Berkeley store scanner data found sugary drink sales fell, but calories purchased per transaction did not change significantly.
People shifted calories rather than cutting them.
Calling a regressive tax "progressive" because the poor change behaviour most just means the poor pay most, in money or in lost choice.
Industry lobbying does not explain Denmark, whose own government scrapped its soft-drink tax in 2014 after shoppers crossed the border.
Your scanner study measured calories per transaction, not total calories bought across the store.

Total sales of sugary drinks in Berkeley fell by 9.6% while sales of untaxed drinks rose, especially water, according to that same 2017 PLOS Medicine study, so substitution was toward healthier options.
Philadelphia's 1.5-cent-per-ounce tax has raised over $100 million for pre-K and community schools, a direct benefit to low-income families.
Mexico's purchases fell further in later years, and WHO continues to recommend such taxes because the long-run effect on obesity emerges as cohorts grow up without sugary drinks from childhood.
A regressive tax that funds progressive services is not a punishment; it is a public health investment.
PRO now defends the tax as a revenue source, and that exposes the contradiction.
Philadelphia's pre-K money depends on poor households continuing to buy soda; if the health goal succeeds, the funding collapses.
Schools deserve stable, broad-based funding, not a levy on the cheapest groceries of low-income families.
Berkeley's water gains are welcome, but they came in a wealthy, health-conscious city of about 120,000.
The large 2019 JAMA study of Philadelphia found much of the city's drop in sales was offset by rising purchases in neighbouring areas.
PRO's last defence is a promise about future cohorts that no data yet confirms.
Denmark tried, measured and repealed.
Governments should pursue education, reformulation and healthcare access instead.
Nuclear power is a proven low-carbon source.
Since 1971, nuclear reactors have avoided over 60 gigatonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, according to the International Energy Agency.
France generates roughly 70 percent of its electricity from nuclear, giving it a carbon intensity far below most industrialized nations.
The Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change finds that scenarios limiting warming to 1.5 degrees Celsius generally require more nuclear power by mid-century.
Building new plants, especially advanced designs, would cut emissions while providing reliable baseload power that variable renewables alone cannot guarantee.
Nuclear is low-carbon, but that does not make new reactors the best way to cut emissions quickly.
Finland’s Olkiluoto 3 began regular electricity production in April 2023, fourteen years later than its original 2009 target.
IPCC’s 2022 mitigation report found that solar and wind unit costs fell 85 percent and 55 percent respectively between 2010 and 2019.
Countries should prioritize technologies they can deploy sooner, alongside grids, storage and demand flexibility.
Keeping safe existing reactors operating is different from committing scarce investment to new construction.
Advanced designs cannot erase the demonstrated schedule risks of building nuclear plants.
Olkiluoto 3 is not representative of all new builds.
France constructed more than fifty reactors between 1974 and 1989, transforming its grid to mostly nuclear.
The United Arab Emirates brought four Korean-designed reactors online from 2021 through 2024.
Falling solar and wind costs do not solve reliability; those sources need storage or backup during calm, dark periods.
The IPCC’s low-warming pathways still expand nuclear, because it delivers firm power at capacity factors above 90 percent in recent years.
Countries should build both renewables and nuclear, not abandon a proven zero-carbon baseload source because of one delayed first-of-a-kind project.
Barakah shows nuclear can be delivered, but construction began in 2012 and its fourth reactor entered commercial operation in 2024.
That is not a quick climate intervention.
Olkiluoto is not the only warning: in January 2024, EDF pushed Hinkley Point C’s first-unit completion estimate to 2029–2031, versus its original 2025 target.
Reliability matters, but high capacity factors do not eliminate construction risk or establish cost-effectiveness.
IPCC pathways are scenarios, not instructions that every country must build reactors.
“Build both” still requires allocating limited money and construction capacity.
My objection is to prioritizing new nuclear, not maintaining safe existing plants.
My opponent cites Hinkley Point C and Barakah as slow.
But Barakah delivered four reactors between 2012 and 2024, about three years per unit on average; serial construction works.
Hinkley is a first-of-a-kind EPR in a new regulatory setting.
China’s Hualong One units have gone from construction start to commercial operation in about six years.
The IPCC’s 1.5°C pathways generally expand nuclear capacity substantially.
Nuclear already provides about 10 percent of global electricity and a quarter of low-carbon electricity.
Countries facing rising electricity demand and decarbonization should build more nuclear plants, not fewer, while also deploying renewables.
Dividing Barakah’s twelve-year programme by four does not establish a three-year construction time: reactors were built concurrently.
Its first unit began construction in 2012 and entered commercial operation in 2021.
China’s faster projects demonstrate possibilities, not timelines every country can reproduce.
Nuclear’s existing contribution is not evidence that new reactors offer the fastest or cheapest additional emissions cuts.
The IPCC’s 2022 mitigation report identifies solar and wind among options with large emissions-reduction potential at low cost by 2030.
Preserve safe existing nuclear, but prioritize rapidly deployable clean electricity, transmission and flexibility rather than make new nuclear construction a general prescription.
Sugar-sweetened drinks deliver large amounts of sugar with almost no nutritional value, and the World Health Organization recommends taxing them to curb obesity, type 2 diabetes and tooth decay.
The evidence shows such taxes work.
Mexico introduced a tax of one peso per litre in 2014.
A study in the BMJ found that purchases of taxed drinks fell by an average of 6 percent in the first year and by 12 percent by December, with larger drops among poorer households.
Britain's Soft Drinks Industry Levy, which took effect in April 2018, pushed many manufacturers to cut sugar before it began, so consumers benefited without changing their habits.
This is a cheap, proven tool, and governments should use it.
Taxing sugary drinks is a regressive burden that delivers modest health gains.
Take PRO's own Mexico example: the BMJ study found purchases fell about 6 percent in 2014, but the drop is small beside the scale of the obesity problem, and Mexican obesity rates have not fallen.
Sugary drinks are only one source of calories, and people can substitute other sweetened foods or cheaper, untaxed sugary products.
The tax also falls hardest on low-income households, who spend a larger share of income on groceries.

If a government wants healthier diets, it should use education, clearer labelling, and school nutrition rules, not a levy that raises prices on everyone, including the many who drink these beverages in moderation.
Taxes should not be used to police personal choices.

CON calls the tax regressive, but the evidence shows the opposite: the same BMJ study found poorer Mexican households cut purchases the most, so they gain the most health benefit, and they also suffer the highest rates of diet-related disease.
Revenue can be returned to them too.
Britain directed levy money to school sport and healthy breakfast programmes.
As for "modest" effects, no single measure ends obesity.
A 6 percent first-year drop that grew over time is a solid result for one policy.
Education and labelling, CON's alternatives, have been tried for decades without reversing obesity.
A tax works alongside them.
Public Health England reported that sugar in levy-liable drinks fell about 29 percent between 2015 and 2018, without anyone policing choices.
PRO says poorer households cut purchases most, but that proves the burden falls on them.
Cutting back means paying a tax or giving up a product they value, and the tax is paid in proportion to what they buy, so it takes a larger share of a small budget.
Whether health gains offset that is unproven; the BMJ study measured purchases, not weight or disease.
Mexico's obesity rate has not fallen, as PRO does not dispute.

The British reformulation success shows something different: it came from a threat to manufacturers, not from taxing consumers, and the levy's tiered structure applied only to drinks above 5 grams of sugar per 100 millilitres.
Reformulation can be encouraged by targeted sugar limits without a broad tax.
Also, "tried for decades" understates school nutrition rules, which are far more recent and under-evaluated.
CON says reformulation came from a threat, not a tax.
But the threat *was* the tax: Britain's levy is what made manufacturers cut sugar, and "targeted limits" without a price signal have no comparable record.
CON also says the evidence covers only purchases, not health.
Yet a 2023 PLOS Medicine study linked the UK levy to roughly an 8 percent relative fall in obesity among year-six girls, with the largest effects in the most deprived areas.
On regressivity, a poor family that switches to water pays nothing.
It keeps its money and gains the health benefit, while levy revenue funds children's sport and breakfasts.
A tax that changes products, changes behaviour and pays for healthier childhoods deserves support.

PRO's best new evidence is the 2023 PLOS Medicine study, but it is a single observational analysis of one age group, year-six girls, and it found no significant effect for boys or for year-two children.
One subgroup result is thin grounds for a national policy.
It also cannot separate the levy from other trends in England.
On the claim that a poor family can simply switch to water: that concedes the point.
A tax that works by forcing people out of a product they chose is a cost on those who keep buying, and many will, because habit and taste are stubborn.
The revenue also goes to general programmes, not back to those who paid.
Britain's levy worked through reformulation, so a narrower tool than a consumer tax is plausible.
Nuclear power is among the cleanest sources of electricity we have.
The IPCC's Fifth Assessment Report put its median lifecycle emissions at 12 grams of CO2 per kilowatt-hour, comparable to wind and lower than solar, while coal sits around 820.
France shows what this means in practice: with roughly two-thirds of its electricity from reactors, its grid emits a fraction of the carbon per kilowatt-hour that Germany's does.
Nuclear is also safe.
Our World in Data estimates about 0.03 deaths per terawatt-hour, versus about 24.6 for coal.
And unlike wind and solar, reactors run day and night regardless of weather.
A serious climate plan needs this firm, clean power.
The motion ignores that nuclear is too slow and costly to cut emissions in the time we have.
Lazard’s 2023 levelized cost analysis puts new nuclear at $141–221 per megawatt-hour, far above utility-scale solar at $24–96 and onshore wind at $24–75.
Real projects confirm this: the two Vogtle units in Georgia, approved in 2009, only came online in 2023–2024 and cost over $30 billion, more than double early estimates.
Hinkley Point C in Britain is years late, now projected around £33 billion.
Every dollar sunk into slow reactors could instead deploy renewables and storage now, cutting carbon faster and cheaper.
Climate urgency demands speed we can measure.
My opponent judges nuclear by its worst Western projects.
Vogtle and Hinkley were first-of-a-kind builds after decades in which those countries built almost no reactors, so supply chains and skilled workforces had withered.
Where nations build steadily, timelines shrink.
France connected dozens of reactors in roughly fifteen years after the 1970s oil shock, decarbonizing most of its grid faster than any country has with renewables.
The UAE's Barakah plant began construction in 2012, and all four units were operating by 2024.
Lazard's cost ranges for solar and wind also exclude the storage and backup needed when weather fails.
A cheap megawatt-hour that arrives at noon does not power a still winter night.
My opponent treats France's 1970s nuclear sprint as repeatable, but it is not.
France's own newest reactor, Flamanville 3, began construction in 2007 and only connected to the grid in December 2024, after long delays and large overruns.
The UAE's Barakah took roughly twelve years from first concrete to full operation.
Solar and wind farms are typically built in one to three years, cutting emissions almost immediately.
Storage is no fatal objection: battery costs have fallen sharply, and combined renewable-plus-storage projects are already undercutting new nuclear in many markets.
Climate targets cannot wait for reactors that break ground today and produce power after 2040.
Flamanville actually proves my point.
France broke ground on it in 2007, a decade after its previous reactor came online, and the lost expertise showed.
Steady building is what keeps costs and timelines down.
Barakah's first unit reached the grid in 2020, about eight years after construction began, and its later units followed faster.
So reactors started this decade need not wait until 2040.
My opponent also offers a false choice.
We should build solar and wind quickly and build reactors, because a grid running only on weather needs huge storage and backup to get through long, still, dark winter spells.
The countries with the cleanest large grids, France and Sweden, rely heavily on nuclear power.
That record, not a forecast, should guide us.
My opponent leans on the 1970s, but today’s nuclear cannot repeat it.
Flamanville took 17 years; Vogtle and Hinkley are on similar paths.
A reactor approved today would likely not cut emissions until the late 2030s, after crucial carbon budgets are spent.
Solar and wind plus batteries go from contract to operation in one to three years.
Clean grids do not require nuclear: Norway and Iceland run almost entirely on hydro and geothermal, while Denmark and Portugal push high renewable shares with storage and interconnectors.
The real false choice is pretending only nuclear can back up renewables; increasingly, cheap storage and flexible demand can.
Countries should build more nuclear power plants because cutting emissions requires replacing fossil-fuel electricity with reliable low-carbon supply.
The IPCC’s 2014 assessment reported median lifecycle emissions of 12 grams of CO₂-equivalent per kilowatt-hour for nuclear power, compared with 820 for coal and 490 for gas.
Those figures include construction and fuel supply, not just plant operation.
Nuclear plants can generate electricity when wind and sunlight are unavailable, complementing renewables rather than competing with them.
Construction costs and delays deserve scrutiny, but rejecting nuclear removes a proven low-carbon option precisely when countries need more options, not fewer.
My opponent is right that nuclear's lifecycle emissions are low.
The problem is time and money, and both matter because emissions cut sooner are worth more.
Georgia's Vogtle units 3 and 4 came online in 2023 and 2024, roughly seven years late, at a total cost above $30 billion, more than double the original estimate.
France's Flamanville 3 began construction in 2007 and connected to the grid only in 2024.
Britain's Hinkley Point C has slipped to around 2030.
Lazard's 2023 analysis put unsubsidized nuclear at $141 to $221 per megawatt-hour, against $24 to $96 for utility solar.
Every dollar sunk into slow reactors buys fewer tonnes of avoided carbon than wind, solar, storage and efficiency deliver now.
Vogtle and Flamanville demonstrate serious project failures, not that every nuclear investment cuts less carbon than alternatives.
The UAE began building Barakah in 2012; its first reactor entered commercial operation in 2021, and all four were operating commercially by September 2024.
Its 5.6-gigawatt capacity shows that countries can deliver substantial nuclear expansion.
Lazard’s generation-cost comparison does not establish the cheapest complete electricity system: solar alone cannot supply electricity at night, and storage adds costs.
Countries should deploy renewables immediately while building nuclear where delivery is credible.
Near-term cuts and long-lived, low-carbon electricity are complementary goals, not mutually exclusive choices.
Barakah proves my point more than my opponent's.

Its first unit was originally scheduled for 2017 and arrived four years late, despite an absolute monarchy, a Korean builder with a standardized design, and a patient state budget few democracies can replicate.
Even best-case nuclear takes around a decade from groundbreaking to full output.
On system costs, Lazard's same 2023 report priced utility solar paired with storage, and that combination still came in below new nuclear.
Meanwhile China, which builds reactors faster than anyone, added far more solar and wind capacity than nuclear in recent years, revealing where the cheapest carbon cuts lie.
Scarce climate dollars should chase tonnes avoided this decade, not prestige projects delivering in the 2030s.
Solar plus storage is not equivalent to continuous supply: costs depend on storage duration and how often batteries must recharge.
China’s larger renewable additions do not establish that nuclear is unnecessary; capacity additions alone ignore electricity production and timing.
I accept Barakah’s delay, but its four reactors now supply low-carbon electricity beyond this decade.
The IEA’s 2022 report, Nuclear Power and Secure Energy Transitions, concluded that less nuclear would make net-zero transitions harder and more expensive.
Build renewables and efficiency now, but also build nuclear where institutions can deliver it.
The motion requires more nuclear, not nuclear instead of renewables or at any price.
My opponent now concedes the motion means nuclear only "where institutions can deliver it" and "not at any price."
Vogtle, Flamanville and Hinkley show that even wealthy democracies often cannot.
